tagline: The Côte d'Azur, the Calanques and Corsica — Europe's premium coastline, still moving on diesel.
summary: France's Mediterranean arc is one of the world's most concentrated luxury-marine markets: the Côte d'Azur from Nice and Antibes to Cannes, the Calanques and old port of Marseille, the Île de Beauté of Corsica, and the short hop to Monaco. It is dense with superyachts, marinas and high-end clientele — and almost entirely served by diesel tenders, ferries and conventional day-boats. A clean, stabilised foiling tier is the premium-but-practical layer this coast has never had.
why_marine_mobility: No single city tells the French Riviera story — it is a corridor of marinas, anchorages and islands strung along the coast and out to Corsica. Today the moves between Nice, Antibes, Cannes, the Lérins islands, Monaco and the Calanques run on diesel tenders and ferries; the Corsica crossing and the long Riviera-to-Sardinia run go by car-ferry. Navier's foiling tier flies the short coastal and island hops smooth, dry, quiet and clean on Pioneer II today, while the Quanta-LR hybrid opens the long open-water trunks — Nice toward Sardinia, and the Corsica crossing — that no battery day-boat can serve.

demand_signals.label: Superyacht & marina density
demand_signals.note: The Côte d'Azur (Monaco, Antibes, Cannes, Saint-Tropez) is one of the world's densest superyacht and marina markets, with a large pool of high-end clientele and tender traffic — a premium water-mobility market that already exists.

demand_signals.label: Island & coastal day-trip volume
demand_signals.note: The Lérins islands off Cannes, the Calanques between Marseille and Cassis, and the Corsica coast draw heavy seasonal day-trip and excursion demand moving on conventional ferries and excursion boats.

demand_signals.label: Marina-network operator presence
demand_signals.note: Large marina-network operators (e.g. D-Marin's Mediterranean footprint) anchor a chain of premium berths across the basin — a natural distribution and berthing partner for a premium foiling tier that rides existing jetties.

use_cases.body: Nice and Antibes to Monaco: the iconic Riviera hop flown smooth and quiet on Pioneer II — a clean premium shuttle for an audience that today moves by tender, helicopter or road.

Cannes to the Îles de Lérins (Sainte-Marguerite): a short, scenic island crossing run today on diesel excursion boats — ideal for a quiet, dry, premium foiling tier, with the Calanques out of Marseille and Cassis as a natural second corridor.

Côte d'Azur to Corsica and Sardinia: the long open-water trunks — Nice toward the Costa Smeralda, and the Corsica crossing — are Quanta-LR corridors no day-boat can reach, linking the Riviera to the islands on a single clean hybrid leg.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The coastal and island hops — Nice/Antibes to Monaco, Cannes to the Lérins islands, Antibes to Cannes, and the Calanques out of Marseille — all sit inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile range at 30 knots, commercial-ready today and a clean upgrade on diesel tenders and excursion boats.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The long open-water trunks — Côte d'Azur (Nice) toward Costa Smeralda / Sardinia (~185 nm) and the Corsica crossing — are Quanta-LR corridors (~700 nm hybrid range, H2 2026+), opening island links no battery day-boat can serve.

signature_routes.label: Nice ↔ Monaco (Port Hercule) — the iconic Riviera hop
Cannes ↔ Îles de Lérins (Sainte-Marguerite) — scenic island crossing
Côte d'Azur (Nice) ↔ Costa Smeralda / Sardinia — long open-water trunk
Côte d'Azur ↔ Corsica (Ajaccio / Bastia) — the Île de Beauté crossing

transit_planning: For a marina-network operator or a premium charter operator: begin with the dense, all-electric Pioneer II coastal hops between Nice, Antibes, Cannes, the Lérins islands and Monaco — a clean, quiet premium tier riding existing berths — then add the long Corsica and Sardinia trunks on Quanta-LR as range comes online. No new shoreside infrastructure is required; the craft uses the existing marina and port network.
competitive_landscape: Riviera marine movement today runs on diesel tenders, conventional ferries and excursion day-boats — capable but loud, fuel-heavy and unremarkable — alongside helicopter for the Monaco hop. There is no clean, on-demand premium water tier matched to this high-end market. Navier's foiling craft is the missing premium-but-practical option: quieter and smoother than a tender, faster than a ferry, and clean enough to suit a coastline under tightening emissions scrutiny.
regulatory_note: French maritime transport is regulated by the Direction des affaires maritimes (Ministère de la Transition écologique) and enforced by the Préfecture maritime de la Méditerranée; passenger operation requires vessel certification and route authorisation. The Calanques National Park imposes navigation and access rules, and Monaco's own port authority governs the Monaco hop — natural early regulatory touchpoints.
seasonality: Peak demand runs late spring through early autumn (May–Sep), aligned with the yachting season, the Cannes and Monaco event calendar and warm calm seas; the mistral wind can bring sharp short-lived chop to the Gulf of Lion and the Corsica channel year-round — conditions where a stabilised foiling craft holds comfort and schedule better than a conventional tender.
